content_of_post_to_comment: You Live in Utopia In 1888 American novelist Edward Bellamy wrote a book set in the year 2000. He was trying to imagine the most wonderful world he could build. Here is the wildest thing he came up with: "If we could have devised an arrangement for providing everybody with music in their homes, perfect in quality, unlimited in quantity, suited to every mood, and beginning and ceasing at will, we should have considered the limit of human felicity already attained." Everything we take for granted was once an otherworldly luxury. The following examples are inspired by a lovely essay called "Ordinary Abundance" by Joseph Davidson. The light switch. In 1880, Wabash, Indiana became one of the first towns in the world lit by electricity. A witness wrote: "The people, almost with bated breath, stood overwhelmed with awe, as if in the presence of the supernatural." A good candle gives you about a hundredth of the light of a single 100-watt bulb. When you open your refrigerator door you summon forth more light than the total amount enjoyed by most households in the 18th century. The tap. In 1842, clean water finally reached New York City. A diarist named Philip Hone wrote: "Water! Water! is the universal note which is sounded through every part of the city, and infuses joy and exultation into the masses." Ten years earlier, cholera had killed 3,515 New Yorkers. The fruit bowl. A pineapple in eighteenth-century Britain cost the equivalent of thousands of pounds. It was too valuable to eat. So people rented them — one pineapple doing the rounds of a dozen dinner parties as a centrepiece, sometimes rotting on tour without anyone ever tasting it. Look at the top of the Wimbledon trophy sometime. That's a pineapple. That's how rich you had to be. Berries are the same story. In 1712 Louis XIV sent a spy to Chile to smuggle out strawberry plants, because the King of France wanted strawberries in March instead of June. In 1989 a California family firm called Driscoll's decided to make all four berries available, in every season, in every part of the world. The bathroom. Patty Doak, recalling her family's first indoor toilet in rural Iowa: "It just felt like I was the wealthiest person in the world. It felt great not to have to go outside to go to the restroom." Your teeth. In the early 1960s, roughly half of Americans aged 65 to 74 had lost every single one of theirs. Go back further and it gets grim: after the Battle of Waterloo, scavengers went through the dead pulling teeth to sell for dentures. Surgery. Every operation in human history before 1846 was performed on a conscious person. On a monument over the man who first demonstrated ether: "Before whom, in all time, surgery was agony." Charles II's fourteen physicians treated his stroke with enemas, purges, plasters made of pigeon droppings and, at the end, an opened jugular vein. Drowning victims fished out of the Thames were revived by having tobacco smoke blown up their backsides, because mouth-to-mouth was considered vulgar. The photo of your kids on your phone. Elizabeth Barrett Browning, on seeing her first photograph in 1843: "The very shadow of the person lying there fixed for ever!… I would rather have such a memorial of one I dearly loved, than the noblest artist's work ever produced." Most families in history had no accurate image of the people they lost. The thermostat. Thomas Jefferson, writing a letter in 1796: "It is so cold that the freezing of the ink on the point of my pen renders it difficult to write." The street outside. A working horse produces about 45 pounds of manure a day. New York had well over a hundred thousand of them. On Liberty Street there was a manure heap seven feet high. One of the main jobs of the horses was pulling the wagons that carried away the horse manure. Five numbers Two hundred years ago in Sweden, one of the healthiest places on earth, about one child in three died before their fifth birthday. Today it's 0.3%. A hundredfold drop. In the 1960s, 14% of children with the most common childhood leukaemia lived five years. By the 2010s, 94% did. Around 1800 in Sweden and Finland, roughly 900 mothers died for every 100,000 births, close to one in a hundred. Most rich countries are now under ten. As Steven Pinker puts it: "for an American woman, being pregnant a century ago was almost as dangerous as having breast cancer today." Age-adjusted dementia in America has fallen 67% in forty years. Four decades ago, three in ten Americans aged 85–89 had it. Now it's about one in ten. Guinea worm is a parasite three and a half thousand years old. It's described in an Egyptian medical scroll from 1550 BC, with the same treatment we used until recently: wrap the worm around a stick and pull it out of the blister in your leg, an inch a day, for weeks. In 1986 it infected 3.5 million people. Last year it infected ten. So why does nobody believe we're living through the best period in human history? Because the good news arrives too slowly to be news. Max Roser points out that for twenty-five years straight, a newspaper could have honestly run the headline "NUMBER OF PEOPLE IN EXTREME POVERTY FELL BY 137,000 SINCE YESTERDAY." Every single day. None ever did, because nothing that happens every day is news. If a newspaper came out once every fifty years, it wouldn't report half a century of celebrity gossip and political scandal. It would report that we'd doubled the human lifespan. Meanwhile, homicides get 40–50% of all news coverage about causes of death. They are under 1% of deaths. And each extra negative word in a headline earns about 2.3% more clicks. The tell is we don't apply any of it to ourselves. Last year, 85% of French people said it had been a bad year for France. Only 45% said it had been a bad year for them. Ask South Koreans what share of their countrymen are happy and they guess 25%. The real number is 90%. And it can get so much better Nearly five million children still died before their fifth birthday last year. And progress cannot be taken for granted. Argentina was one of the ten richest countries on earth a century ago and is now somewhere around seventy-fifth. Nothing about this is guaranteed, or owed to us. Those are real problems. They are also solvable, which is exactly the point. Do you know how guinea worm was eliminated? In 1986 some people decided to kill it, handed out cheap cloth water filters, and then walked from village to village for forty years. From 3.5 million cases to ten. When it hits zero it will be the second disease humans have ever wiped off the planet, and the first ever ended without a single dose of medicine. The pineapple got cheap because people spent two centuries working on ships, greenhouses and refrigeration. Berries are in your fridge in February because Driscoll's wrote it down as a goal in 1989 and then spent 35 years doing it. Your tap runs clean because New York built an aqueduct. Pessimists sound smart. Rational optimists build the future.
